qs.q: A 52-year-old man undergoes an elective sigmoid colectomy for diverticular disease. On the third postoperative day, he develops severe lower abdominal pain and a high-grade fever. Which category of postoperative complication does this most likely represent?
o: Classify as a later postoperative complication.
Label it a delayed structural defect.
Identify it as an immediate/early complication.
Consider it a chronic functional impairment.
qs.e: Postoperative complications such as infections occurring days after surgery are classified as immediate or early complications. Later complications typically include incisional hernias and adhesive intestinal obstructions.

qs.q: A 70-year-old nursing home resident with chronic immobility presents with lower abdominal pain and a hard mass of stool obstructing the distal bowel. What is the most likely cause of obstruction in this patient?
qs.e: Faecal impaction involves a hard mass of stool obstructing the distal bowel, particularly in elderly, immobile, or chronically constipated patients.

qs.q: A 72-year-old institutionalized man with Parkinson disease presents with rapid, massive abdominal distension, absolute constipation, and acute colicky lower abdominal pain. His abdomen is tense, tympanitic, and drum-like with an empty rectum on digital examination. There is no rebound tenderness or guarding. What is the most common underlying predisposing factor for this condition in African hospi
o: Prior abdominal surgery and peritoneal adhesions
Malignant stricture of the descending colon
A high-fibre diet with a long redundant sigmoid
Congenital aganglionic megacolon of the rectum
qs.e: Sigmoid volvulus is commonly predisposed to by a high-fibre diet leading to a bulky stool load and a long redundant sigmoid colon with a narrow-based mesentery. In African hospitals, it accounts for over 50% of intestinal obstructions, unlike Western nations where cancer is more frequent.
qs.s: Sigmoid and Caecal Volvulus: Diagnosis and Management: MCQs

qs.q: An 80-year-old man presents with generalized peritonism, guarding, and rebound tenderness following three days of colicky lower abdominal pain and absolute constipation. At emergency laparotomy, the sigmoid colon is found to be gangrenous and non-viable. What is the most appropriate surgical procedure for this unstable patient?
o: Sigmoid colectomy combined with a Hartmann procedure
Simple detorsion with sigmoidopexy and tube drainage
Resection with primary on-table lavage and anastomosis
qs.e: In an unstable patient with gangrene, perforation, or peritonitis, a sigmoid colectomy with Hartmann's procedure is the safest option. Primary anastomosis is reserved for stable patients with viable bowel.
qs.s: Sigmoid and Caecal Volvulus: Diagnosis and Management: MCQs

qs.q: A 28-year-old woman presents with sudden onset of severe lower abdominal pain and dizziness. Her history reveals a missed menstrual period. Which underlying mechanism of acute abdomen is most likely responsible for her presentation?
qs.e: A ruptured ectopic pregnancy causes haemorrhage and presents with sudden abdominal pain and a history of missed menses. Inflammation typically causes a more gradual onset of symptoms rather than a sudden vascular or haemorrhagic collapse.

qs.q: A 24-year-old woman presents with acute lower abdominal pain. Which imaging modality is most useful for identifying gallstones, cholecystitis, suspected ectopic pregnancy, or pelvic pathology?
qs.e: Ultrasound is useful for gallstones, cholecystitis, suspected ectopic pregnancy, pelvic pathology, selected appendicitis cases, and free fluid. Computed tomography is preferred for obstruction and perforation.

qs.q: A 25-year-old woman with lower abdominal pain and vaginal bleeding is evaluated in the emergency department. Which condition must be excluded first as a potentially life-threatening differential diagnosis?
qs.e: In a patient who could be pregnant, pregnancy testing is important because ectopic pregnancy is a potentially life-threatening differential diagnosis. Gastroenteritis does not carry the same immediate surgical emergency profile in this context.

qs.q: A 29-year-old woman with a positive pregnancy test presents with severe lower abdominal pain and dizziness. What is the immediate priority during her initial clinical assessment?
o: Calculating the estimated date of delivery by Naegele's rule
Urgent assessment for ectopic pregnancy or haemorrhage
Scheduling a routine anomaly scan at 20 weeks
Initiating oral iron supplementation for physiological anaemia
qs.e: A patient with a positive pregnancy test presenting with abdominal pain and dizziness requires urgent assessment for life-threatening conditions such as ectopic pregnancy or haemorrhage. Routine antenatal scheduling is secondary to acute stabilisation.
qs.s: Obstetrics: Normal Pregnancy and Antenatal Care: MCQs

ai.subject: Obstetrics & gynaecology
ai.summary: Lower abdominal pain in women often signals reproductive tract pathology. Prompt assessment of history, exam and targeted tests guides urgent treatment to prevent infertility, ectopic pregnancy or sepsis.

sections.p: Lower abdominal pain refers to discomfort below the umbilicus, frequently arising from gynecologic organs. Diagnosis combines history, pelvic exam (including cervical motion tenderness), and focused investigations.
b: Pain location, onset, relation to menses, sexual activity, discharge, urinary or gastrointestinal symptoms.
Cervical motion tenderness strongly suggests pelvic inflammatory disease (PID).

sections.p: Severity is graded by pain intensity, systemic signs, and peritoneal irritation. PID uses CDC stages: mild (outpatient), moderate (hospital observation), severe (inpatient, possible sepsis).
b: Mild: no fever, tolerable pain, no rebound.
Moderate: fever ≥38°C, moderate pain, limited guarding.
Severe: high fever, rebound, guarding, hemodynamic instability.

sections.p: Causes are grouped by organ system and epidemiology. In low‑resource settings, infections and obstetric emergencies dominate.
b: Gynecologic infection: PID (N. gonorrhoeae, C. trachomatis, anaerobes).
Early pregnancy loss: threatened/inevitable abortion, ectopic pregnancy.
Obstetric complications: abruptio placentae, uterine rupture (late pregnancy).
Non‑infectious: ovarian torsion, ruptured ovarian cyst, endometriosis.
Urinary: acute cystitis, pyelonephritis.
Gastrointestinal: appendicitis, colitis, intestinal TB.

sections.p: Patients describe dull to severe cramping, often worsened by movement or intercourse. Associated features point to the underlying cause.
b: PID: cervical motion tenderness, purulent discharge, fever.
Ectopic pregnancy: unilateral pain, vaginal spotting, dizziness.
Abortive miscarriage: heavy bleeding, tissue passage.
Ovarian torsion: sudden unilateral pain, nausea, no fever.
Urinary infection: dysuria, frequency, low‑grade fever.

sections.p: Select tests that answer specific clinical questions; adapt when resources are limited.

t.b: Is the patient pregnant? Positive result mandates obstetric evaluation; negative directs focus to non‑pregnancy causes.
Is there an intrauterine gestation or adnexal mass? Detects ectopic pregnancy, ovarian cyst, or retained products.
Is there infection or anemia? Leukocytosis supports PID/sepsis; low hemoglobin suggests hemorrhage.

t.a: Cervical swabs for Gram stain, NAAT for gonorrhoea/chlamydia
t.b: Which pathogen is causing PID? Guides antibiotic choice; if unavailable, treat empirically for both.
Is urinary tract infection present? Pyuria or bacteriuria confirms cystitis/pyelonephritis.
What is the gestational age? Helps differentiate early intrauterine pregnancy from ectopic.

sections.p: Identify life‑threatening conditions early to initiate urgent care.
b: Hemodynamic instability (pulse >120, BP <90/60).
Severe abdominal guarding/rebound suggesting peritonitis.
Persistent high fever (>38.5°C) despite antibiotics.
Signs of ruptured ectopic pregnancy: sudden shock, abdominal distension.

sections.p: Treat the underlying cause first, then provide supportive care. Use broad‑spectrum regimens when specific pathogens are unknown.
b: PID: ceftriaxone IM + doxycycline PO + metronidazole PO – covers gonorrhoea, chlamydia, anaerobes.
Ectopic pregnancy: urgent surgical removal or methotrexate if stable and small.
Miscarriage with heavy bleeding: suction curettage, blood replacement if needed.
Ovarian torsion: laparoscopy to detorse or remove ovary.
UTI/pyelonephritis: oral/IV fluoroquinolone or third‑generation cephalosporin.

sections.p: Re‑evaluate symptoms after 48‑72 h; ensure completion of therapy and address risk factors.
b: Repeat pelvic exam for PID to confirm resolution.
Counsel on condom use, STI screening for partners.
Vaccinate against HPV and hepatitis B where applicable.
Educate on early pregnancy recognition and when to seek care.

sections.p: Conditions that mimic lower abdominal pain but require different management.
b: Appendicitis – right lower quadrant pain, no cervical tenderness.
Diverticulitis – older patients, left lower quadrant, no gynecologic signs.
Irritable bowel syndrome – chronic, no systemic signs.
Renal colic – flank pain radiating to groin, hematuria.

sections.p: Be aware of false‑negative or non‑specific findings.
b: Early ectopic pregnancy may have low hCG and no ultrasound mass.
Chlamydia NAAT can be negative if specimen collected improperly.
CBC may be normal early in sepsis; rely on clinical picture.

whenToSeekHelp: Severe abdominal guarding or rebound tenderness
Sudden drop in blood pressure or fainting

faq.q: What is the first step when a woman with lower abdominal pain presents?
faq.a: Obtain a pregnancy test to rule in/out obstetric emergencies before other work‑up.

faq.q: Why give three antibiotics for PID?
faq.a: Ceftriaxone targets gonorrhoea, doxycycline covers chlamydia, and metronidazole treats anaerobic bacteria common in polymicrobial infection.

faq.q: When can PID be managed as an outpatient?
faq.a: When pain is mild, vitals are stable, no gastrointestinal signs, and the patient can adhere to oral therapy.

exam: Explain how you would differentiate PID from an ectopic pregnancy in a woman of reproductive age presenting with lower abdominal pain.
List the CDC recommended empirical antibiotic regimen for acute PID and justify each component.
Describe the red‑flag signs that mandate immediate surgical intervention in lower abdominal pain.
